senses: Art that depicts subjects related to paleontology.
The primitive art of Paleolithic peoples.
ety: Coined by American artist Mark Hallett in 1987, from paleo- + art.

senses: A fried crispy, layered sweet pastry filled with fruits or soaked with sugar syrup, popular in northern India.
Dandruff—scaly white dead skin flakes from the human scalp.
Hair follicles and dead skin shed from mammals.
Allergen particles that accumulate on and may be shed from the skin and fur of domestic animals, especially from household pets such as cats and dogs.
To chaperon or shepherd.
examples: Given the vivacious young redhead's attractiveness, some might have assumed he had more than simply professional reasons for sheepdogging her career, but they would have been wrong. He'd seen something in her ...
On June 14, with Kennedy personally sheepdogging it, the No Child Left Behind Act passed the Senate ninety-one to eight.

senses: A non-permanent marker pen.
ety: From the name of the Japanese company Pentel Co., Ltd., which invented the non-permanent marker; ultimately from pen + tell.
examples: Failing this, a piece of hardboard with white Fablon from Woolworths makes a good surface for drawing with water-soluble pentels. The drawings can be removed with a damp cloth.

senses: A Dutch earl or count.
ety: From Dutch graaf. Doublet of graf and grave.
examples: And so the graafs mounted their huge steeds and fled, breaking through the enemy lines.

senses: Having an affinity for lipids; lipophilic.

A wedge-shaped kerbstone that allows a vehicle to enter a driveway without a bump
ety: From lay + back (presumably from confusion between lay and lie).
examples: Mirai Nagasu, like Zhang a promising 14-year-old, showed equally astonishing flexibility on a layback spin Wednesday, leaning so far that the back of her head nearly touched her backside.

senses: Having valves.
To be played by plucking the strings instead of using the bow.
ety: Borrowed from Italian pizzicato, past participle of pizzicare (“to pluck”).

senses: A benign act.
ety: From Middle English benignite, from Middle French benignité (modern French bénignité), from Latin benignitās. By surface analysis, benign + -ity.

A news broadcasting network.

The act of unloading into a lighter, or of conveying by a lighter.

Moreover, as the traffic would be mainly morning and evening rush-hour services, at other times of the day much lighterage across the river could be saved by using part of the new terminus for freight trafic.

senses: Strict adherence to a text, especially to the Bible.
Textual criticism, especially that of the Bible.
Indonesian meatball.
ety: From Indonesian bakso, from Hokkien 肉酥 (bah-so͘).

senses: Overseen by a jury
examples: I had my doubts. I knew that it was not a juried show — in other words that everything sent in had been exhibited.

senses: An unglazed earthenware casserole dish.
ety: From French (à la) diable, from diable (“devil”), from Old French. Doublet of devil, diablo, and diabolus.

senses: Having the characteristics of a sheep, as meekness, shyness, or docility.
Shy, meek, ashamed or embarrassed.
ety: From Middle English schepische, shepisse, shepisshe; equivalent to sheep + -ish.

senses: Serving to propel
ety: Formed from Latin prōpulsus with the suffix -ive.

senses: Serving to condemn or censure.
ety: From Latin condemnāt-, past participle stem of condemnāre + -ory.

senses: the act of entrusting
A group of riders formed during a cycling road race; especially, the main group of riders; the pack.
ety: Borrowed from French peloton (“small ball (of thread, etc.), pellet; (cycling) group of riders formed during a cycling road race; (military) small group of soldiers, platoon”), from pelote (“small ball (of thread, etc.)”) (ultimately from Latin pila (“ball; ball game; globe, sphere”) (probably referring to a ball of hair), from pilus (“strand of hair”), of uncertain origin) + -on (augmentative suffix). Doublet of platoon.

senses: A cocktail made with champagne and cranberry juice.
ety: From Late Latin hibiscus, from Latin hibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos, “marsh mallow”), probably ultimately from Gaulish.

senses: Having nerves of a specified kind.

One thousandth (10⁻³) of a watt, an amount of power that can power a small electronic device such as a single microchip. (Consuming 1 milliwatt during a duration of 1 hour consumes 1 milliwatt-hour of energy.).

Capable of, or suitable for, release.
One who exhibits characteristics or qualities of rural life, or ruralism.
Causing annoyance or pain; irritating.

senses: A hip-hop dance generally performed by moving one's body in a shimmy style and passing a hand through or near the hair on one's own head.
ety: From Dougie. Named after 1980s rapper Doug E. Fresh who performed similar moves.

senses: One billion hertz, 10⁹ Hz.

Enticing or tantalizing.

senses: The part of a laser printer that melts the toner onto the medium.
Quality of being indigenous; membership of an indigenous group.
One who or that which paralyzes
examples: Allergan, the company that turned an obscure muscle paralyzer for eyelid spasms, Botox, into a blockbuster wrinkle smoother, hopes to perform cosmetic alchemy yet again.

senses: In a large professional kitchen, a cook responsible for preparing sauces and for sauteing foods on demand.
A bowl-shaped pan used for sauces and other cookery.
ety: Borrowed from French saucier, from sauce + -ier.

senses: Any object that resembles one half of a pair of pincers.
ety: From Middle English pynsor, from Old French pinceure, pinchure, from pincier (“to pinch”).
